claim: Dopamine plays a role in motor control, as suggested by clues from human movement disorders.
source: Clues from human movement disorders have long suggested that the neurotransmitter dopamine plays a role in motor control, but how the endogenous dopaminergic system influences movement is unknown.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from clinical observations of movement disorders.

claim: Animals were trained to initiate licking after a self-timed interval following a start-timing cue.
source: Animals were trained to initiate licking after a self-timed interval following a start-timing cue; reward was delivered in response to movements initiated after a criterion time.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and training procedure used in the study.

claim: The movement time was variable from trial-to-trial.
source: The movement time was variable from trial-to-trial, as expected from previous studies.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data, consistent with prior literature.

claim: Dopaminergic signals ramped-up over seconds between the start-timing cue and the self-timed movement.
source: Surprisingly, dopaminergic signals ramped-up over seconds between the start-timing cue and the self-timed movement, with variable dynamics that predicted the movement/reward time on single trials.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the photometry recordings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Steeply rising dopaminergic signals preceded early lick-initiation.
source: Steeply rising signals preceded early lick-initiation, whereas slowly rising signals preceded later initiation.
evidence: This describes the relationship between signal dynamics and behavior observed in the data.

claim: Higher baseline dopaminergic signals predicted earlier self-timed movements.
source: Higher baseline signals also predicted earlier self-timed movements.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis showing correlation between baseline signals and movement timing.

claim: Optogenetic activation of dopamine neurons during self-timing did not trigger immediate movements.
source: Optogenetic activation of dopamine neurons during self-timing did not trigger immediate movements, but rather caused systematic early-shifting of movement initiation, whereas inhibition caused late-shifting, as if modulating the probability of movement.
evidence: This describes the results of optogenetic manipulation experiments.

claim: Optogenetic activation of dopamine neurons caused systematic early-shifting of movement initiation.
source: Optogenetic activation of dopamine neurons during self-timing did not trigger immediate movements, but rather caused systematic early-shifting of movement initiation, whereas inhibition caused late-shifting, as if modulating the probability of movement.
evidence: This is a finding from the optogenetic experiments.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of dopamine neurons caused late-shifting of movement initiation.
source: Optogenetic activation of dopamine neurons during self-timing did not trigger immediate movements, but rather caused systematic early-shifting of movement initiation, whereas inhibition caused late-shifting, as if modulating the probability of movement.
evidence: This is a finding from the optogenetic experiments.

claim: The dynamics of endogenous dopaminergic signals quantitatively predicted the moment-by-moment probability of movement initiation on single trials.
source: Consistent with this view, the dynamics of the endogenous dopaminergic signals quantitatively predicted the moment-by-moment probability of movement initiation on single trials.
evidence: This is a finding from the probabilistic modeling analysis of the data.

claim: Ramping dopaminergic signals likely encode dynamic reward expectation.
source: We propose that ramping dopaminergic signals, likely encoding dynamic reward expectation, can modulate the decision of when to move.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings based on the experimental context and prior knowledge.

claim: Ramping dopaminergic signals can modulate the decision of when to move.
source: We propose that ramping dopaminergic signals, likely encoding dynamic reward expectation, can modulate the decision of when to move.
evidence: This is the main conclusion proposed by the authors based on their experimental findings.

claim: Patients with Parkinson's Disease experience difficulty self-initiating movements.
source: Patients and animal models of Parkinson's Disease experience difficulty self-initiating movements, exemplified by perseveration (Hughes et al., 2013), trouble initiating steps when walking (Bloxham et al., 1984), and problems timing movements (Malapani et al., 1998; Meck, 1986; Meck, 2006; Mikhael and Gershman, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior clinical and experimental studies.

claim: Externally cued reactions are often less severely affected in Parkinson's than self-generated actions.
source: In contrast to these self-generated actions, externally cued reactions are often less severely affected in Parkinson's, a phenomenon sometimes referred to as 'paradoxical kinesia' (Barthel et al., 2018; Bloxham et al., 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior clinical studies.

claim: The underlying neuropathophysiology of Parkinson's includes the loss of midbrain dopaminergic neurons.
source: Because the underlying neuropathophysiology of Parkinson's includes the loss of midbrain dopaminergic neurons (DANs), the symptomatology of Parkinson's suggests DAN activity plays an important role in deciding when to self-initiate movement.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Parkinson's disease pathology.

claim: Pharmacological manipulations of dopamine causally and bidirectionally influence movement timing.
source: Indeed, pharmacological manipulations of the neurotransmitter dopamine causally and bidirectionally influence movement timing (Dews and Morse, 1958; Lustig and Meck, 2005; Meck, 1986; Mikhael and Gershman, 2019; Schuster and Zimmerman, 1961).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior pharmacological studies.

claim: Decreased dopamine availability/efficacy generally produces late-shifted movements in self-timed movement tasks.
source: In such self-timed movement tasks, decreased dopamine availability/efficacy (e.g., Parkinson's, neuroleptic drugs) generally produces late-shifted movements (Malapani et al., 1998; Meck, 1986; Meck, 2006; Merchant et al., 2013), whereas high dopamine conditions (e.g., amphetamines) produce early-shifting (Dews and Morse, 1958; Schuster and Zimmerman, 1961).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on dopamine and timing.

claim: High dopamine conditions produce early-shifting of movements in self-timed movement tasks.
source: In such self-timed movement tasks, decreased dopamine availability/efficacy (e.g., Parkinson's, neuroleptic drugs) generally produces late-shifted movements (Malapani et al., 1998; Meck, 1986; Meck, 2006; Merchant et al., 2013), whereas high dopamine conditions (e.g., amphetamines) produce early-shifting (Dews and Morse, 1958; Schuster and Zimmerman, 1961).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on dopamine and timing.

claim: DANs densely innervate the striatum.
source: DANs densely innervate the striatum, where they modulate the activity of spiny projection neurons of the direct and indirect pathways, which are thought to exert a push-pull influence on movement centers (Albin et al., 1989; DeLong, 1990; Freeze et al., 2013; Grillner and Robertson, 2016).
evidence: This is established anatomical and functional knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Phasic bursts of dopaminergic activity have been observed just prior to movement onset (within ~500ms).
source: For example, phasic bursts of dopaminergic activity have been observed just prior to movement onset (within ~500ms; Coddington and Dudman, 2018; Coddington and Dudman, 2019; da Silva et al., 2018; Dodson et al., 2016; Howe and Dombeck, 2016; Wang and Tsien, 2011), and dopaminergic signals have been reported to reflect more general encoding of movement kinematics (Barter et al., 2015; Engelhard et al., 2019; Parker et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on dopaminergic activity.

claim: Optogenetic activation of dopamine neurons within physiological range does not elicit immediate movements.
source: However, optogenetic activation of dopamine neurons—within physiological range—does not elicit immediate movements (Coddington and Dudman, 2018; Coddington and Dudman, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior optogenetic studies.

claim: The distribution of first-lick timing was broadly distributed over several seconds.
source: As expected from previous studies, the distribution of first-lick timing was broadly distributed over several seconds, and exhibited the canonical scalar property of timing, as described by Weber's Law (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B; Gallistel and Gibbon, 2000).
evidence: This is an observation from the behavioral data shown in Figure 1B and supplementary figures, consistent with prior literature.

claim: The first-lick timing distributions exhibited the canonical scalar property of timing, as described by Weber's Law.
source: As expected from previous studies, the distribution of first-lick timing was broadly distributed over several seconds, and exhibited the canonical scalar property of timing, as described by Weber's Law (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B; Gallistel and Gibbon, 2000).
evidence: This is an observation from the behavioral data shown in Figure 1B and supplementary figures, with citation to Weber's Law.

claim: After training, the hazard function for the animals peaked near the target time.
source: However, after training, the hazard function for our animals peaked near the target time (either 3.3 or 5 s), suggesting an accurate latent timing process reflected in the instantaneous movement probability (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is an observation from the hazard function analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: DAN GCaMP6f fluorescence exhibited brief transients following cue onset and immediately before first-lick onset.
source: DAN GCaMP6f fluorescence typically exhibited brief transients following cue onset and immediately before first-lick onset (Figure 2A), as observed in previous studies (Coddington and Dudman, 2018; da Silva et al., 2018; Dodson et al., 2016; Howe and Dombeck, 2016; Schultz et al., 1997).
evidence: This is an observation from the photometry data shown in Figure 2A, consistent with prior studies.

claim: During the timed interval, slow 'ramping up' of fluorescence over seconds was observed, with a minimum after the cue-aligned transient and maximum just before the lick-related transient.
source: However, during the timed interval, we observed slow 'ramping up' of fluorescence over seconds, with a minimum after the cue-aligned transient and maximum just before the lick-related transient.
evidence: This is an observation from the photometry data.

claim: The relatively fast intrinsic decay kinetics of GCaMP6f (t1/2 <100 ms at 37°) should not produce appreciable signal integration over the seconds-long timescales of the ramps observed.
source: The relatively fast intrinsic decay kinetics of GCaMP6f (t1/2 <100 ms at 37°; Helassa et al., 2016) should not produce appreciable signal integration over the seconds-long timescales of the ramps we observed.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known kinetics of GCaMP6f cited from prior literature.

claim: Trials with early first-licks exhibited steep ramping of dopaminergic signals.
source: Trials with early first-licks exhibited steep ramping, whereas trials with later first-licks started from lower fluorescence levels and rose more slowly toward the time of movement.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis comparing signals across different movement times.

claim: Trials with later first-licks started from lower fluorescence levels and rose more slowly toward the time of movement.
source: Trials with early first-licks exhibited steep ramping, whereas trials with later first-licks started from lower fluorescence levels and rose more slowly toward the time of movement.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis comparing signals across different movement times.

claim: The fluorescence ramps terminated at nearly the same amplitude, regardless of the movement time.
source: The fluorescence ramps terminated at nearly the same amplitude, regardless of the movement time.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: Ramping dynamics were not evident in control tdTomato signals.
source: Ramping dynamics were not evident in control tdTomato signals (Figure 2C), indicating that the ramping in the GCaMP6f signals was not an optical artifact.
evidence: This is an observation from the control channel data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Average DAN GCaMP6f signals were correlated with first-lick timing even before cue-onset, with higher baseline fluorescence predicting earlier first-licks.
source: In addition to ramping dynamics, average DAN GCaMP6f signals were correlated with first-lick timing even before cue-onset, with higher baseline fluorescence predicting earlier first-licks (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: The correlation between baseline fluorescence and first-lick timing began before the lamp-off event (Pearson's r = −0.63, 95% CI=[-0.92,–0.14], n = 12 mice).
source: This correlation began before the lamp-off event (the 2 s 'Baseline' period before lamp-off; Pearson's r = −0.63 (95% CI=[-0.92,–0.14]), n = 12 mice) and grew stronger during the 'Lamp-Off Interval' between lamp-off and the cue (Pearson's r = −0.89 (95% CI=[-0.98,–0.68]), n = 12 mice; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: The correlation between baseline fluorescence and first-lick timing grew stronger during the 'Lamp-Off Interval' between lamp-off and the cue (Pearson's r = −0.89, 95% CI=[-0.98,–0.68], n = 12 mice).
source: This correlation began before the lamp-off event (the 2 s 'Baseline' period before lamp-off; Pearson's r = −0.63 (95% CI=[-0.92,–0.14]), n = 12 mice) and grew stronger during the 'Lamp-Off Interval' between lamp-off and the cue (Pearson's r = −0.89 (95% CI=[-0.98,–0.68]), n = 12 mice; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Similar ramping dynamics were found in SNc DAN axon terminals in the dorsolateral striatum (DLS).
source: We found similar ramping dynamics in SNc DAN axon terminals in the dorsolateral striatum (DLS; Figure 2—figure supplement 3A-B) at a location involved in goal-directed licking behavior (Sippy et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an observation from the photometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A-B.

claim: Ramping was present in GCaMP6f-expressing DAN cell bodies in the ventral tegmental area (VTA).
source: Ramping was also present in GCaMP6f-expressing DAN cell bodies in the ventral tegmental area (VTA, Figure 2—figure supplement 3C), reminiscent of mesolimbic ramping signals described in goal-oriented navigation tasks (Howe et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an observation from the photometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C, with comparison to prior studies.

claim: Both dLight1.1 and DA2m dopamine sensors revealed similar timing-related ramping dynamics on average.
source: The decay kinetics of the two extracellular dopamine sensors differ somewhat (Patriarchi et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2020), which we confirmed (dLight1.1 t1/2~75 ms, DA2m t1/2~125 ms; Figure 3—figure supplement 1), yet both revealed similar timing-related ramping dynamics on average (Figure 3 inset).
evidence: This is an observation from the dopamine sensor data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The seconds-long dopaminergic ramping signals were not artifacts of sluggish temporal responses of the various fluorescent sensors.
source: These combined data argue that the seconds-long dopaminergic ramping signals were not artifacts of sluggish temporal responses of the various fluorescent sensors and were ultimately expressed as ramp-like increases in dopamine release in the striatum.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined observations from multiple sensors with different kinetics.

claim: The systematic ramping dynamics and baseline differences were not observed in the tdTomato optical control channel nor in any of the other movement-control channels, at least on average.
source: The systematic ramping dynamics and baseline differences were not observed in the tdTomato optical control channel nor in any of the other movement-control channels, at least on average (Figure 4), making it unlikely that ramping dynamics resulted from optical artifacts.
evidence: This is an observation from the control channel data shown in Figure 4.

claim: A nested generalized linear encoding model of single-trial GCaMP6f signals robustly detected task-event GCaMP6f kernels locked to cue, lick and EMG/accelerometer events.
source: We thus derived a nested generalized linear encoding model of single-trial GCaMP6f signals (Engelhard et al., 2019; Park et al., 2014; Runyan et al., 2017), a data-driven, statistical approach designed to isolate and quantify the contributions of task events (timing-independent predictors) from processes predictive of movement timing (timing-dependent predictors; Figure 5A–B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-D). The model robustly detected task-event GCaMP6f kernels locked to cue, lick and EMG/accelerometer events, but these timing-independent predictors alone were insufficient to capture the rich variability of GCaMP6f signals for trials with different first-lick times, especially the timing-dependent ramp-slope and baseline offset (n = 12 mice, Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E-G).
evidence: This is a finding from the GLM analysis shown in Figure 5 and supplementary figures.

claim: Timing-independent predictors alone were insufficient to capture the rich variability of GCaMP6f signals for trials with different first-lick times.
source: The model robustly detected task-event GCaMP6f kernels locked to cue, lick and EMG/accelerometer events, but these timing-independent predictors alone were insufficient to capture the rich variability of GCaMP6f signals for trials with different first-lick times, especially the timing-dependent ramp-slope and baseline offset (n = 12 mice, Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E-G).
evidence: This is a finding from the GLM analysis shown in Figure 5C and supplementary figures.

claim: Two timing-dependent predictors robustly improved the model: a baseline offset with amplitude linearly proportional to first-lick time, and a 'stretch' feature representing percentages of the timed interval.
source: In contrast, two timing-dependent predictors robustly improved the model: (1) a baseline offset with amplitude linearly proportional to first-lick time; and (2) a 'stretch' feature representing percentages of the timed interval (Figure 5B–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a finding from the GLM analysis shown in Figure 5B-C and supplementary figures.

claim: When the same GLM was applied to the tdTomato control signal, timing-dependent predictors did not improve the model.
source: In contrast to the GCaMP6f model, when the same GLM was applied to the tdTomato control signal, the timing-independent predictors (which could potentially cause optical/mechanical artifacts—the cue onset, first-lick, and EMG/accelerometer signal) improved the model, but timing-dependent predictors did not (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F-H).
evidence: This is a finding from the GLM analysis of the control channel shown in Figure 5C and supplementary figures.

claim: Principal component analysis revealed ramp-like and baseline-offset-like components that explained as much as 93% of the variance in DAN signals during the timing interval (mean: 66%, range: 16–93%).
source: In addition, separate principal component (PC) analysis revealed ramp-like and baseline-offset-like components that explained as much as 93% of the variance in DAN signals during the timing interval (mean: 66%, range: 16–93%), but similar PCs were not present when tdTomato control signals were analyzed with PCA (mean variance explained: 4%, range: 1.6–15%, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the PCA analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Similar PCs were not present when tdTomato control signals were analyzed with PCA (mean variance explained: 4%, range: 1.6–15%).
source: In addition, separate principal component (PC) analysis revealed ramp-like and baseline-offset-like components that explained as much as 93% of the variance in DAN signals during the timing interval (mean: 66%, range: 16–93%), but similar PCs were not present when tdTomato control signals were analyzed with PCA (mean variance explained: 4%, range: 1.6–15%, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the PCA analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Single-trial GCaMP6f signals were predictive of first-lick time even for low thresholds intersecting the 'base' of the ramp, with the predictive value of the model progressively improving for higher thresholds (n = 12 mice: mean R2 low = 0.54, mid = 0.71, high = 0.82).
source: Using a simple threshold-crossing decoding model (Maimon and Assad, 2006), we found that single-trial GCaMP6f signals were predictive of first-lick time even for low thresholds intersecting the 'base' of the ramp, with the predictive value of the model progressively improving for higher thresholds (n = 12 mice: mean R2 low = 0.54, mid = 0.71, high = 0.82 (95% CI: low=[0.44,0.64], mid=[0.68,0.75], high=[0.76,0.87]); analysis for one mouse shown in Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a finding from the threshold-crossing decoding model shown in Figure 6A.

claim: GCaMP6f threshold-crossing time dominated every version of the decoding model.
source: All predictors contributed to the predictive power of the model. However, even when we accounted for the contributions of prior trial history, tdTomato artifacts and baseline GCaMP6f signals, GCaMP6f threshold-crossing time robustly dominated the model and absorbed much of the variance explained by baseline dopaminergic signals, alone explaining 10% of the variance in first-lick time on average (range: 1–27%, Figure 6B–D).
evidence: This is a finding from the nested decoding model analysis shown in Figure 6B-D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: GCaMP6f threshold-crossing time alone explained 10% of the variance in first-lick time on average (range: 1–27%).
source: However, even when we accounted for the contributions of prior trial history, tdTomato artifacts and baseline GCaMP6f signals, GCaMP6f threshold-crossing time robustly dominated the model and absorbed much of the variance explained by baseline dopaminergic signals, alone explaining 10% of the variance in first-lick time on average (range: 1–27%, Figure 6B–D).
evidence: This is a finding from the nested decoding model analysis shown in Figure 6B-D.

claim: The slope of the relationship between threshold-crossing time and first-lick time increased markedly as the threshold level was increased, consistent with the ramp model (n = 12 mice: mean slope low = 0.46, mid = 0.7, high = 0.82).
source: We found that the slope of this relationship increased markedly as the threshold level was increased, consistent with the ramp model (n = 12 mice: mean slope low = 0.46, mid = 0.7, high = 0.82 (95% CI: low=[0.37,0.54], mid=[0.66,0.73], high=[0.74,0.88]), Figure 6—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the threshold-crossing analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3C, supporting the ramp model over the step model.

claim: Aligning single-trial GCaMP6f signals according to the optimal step position determined from a Bayesian step model and averaging did not produce a clear step function, but rather yielded a sharp transient superimposed on a 'background' ramping signal.
source: We thus aligned single-trial GCaMP6f signals according to that optimal step position determined from a Bayesian step model fit for each trial and then averaged the step-aligned signals across trials. The averaged signals did not resemble a step function, but rather yielded a sharp transient superimposed on a 'background' ramping signal (Figure 6—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from the step-aligned analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4A, arguing against a discrete step model.

claim: The signal variance showed a monotonic downward trend during the timed interval, with a minimum variance at the time of movement rather than at the point at which 50% of steps had occurred among trials, inconsistent with the discrete step model.
source: The signal variance showed a monotonic downward trend during the timed interval, with a minimum variance at the time of movement rather than at the point at which 50% of steps had occurred among trials, inconsistent with the discrete step model (Figure 6—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from the variance analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4B, arguing against a discrete step model.

claim: DAN activation significantly early-shifted the distribution of self-timed movements on stimulated trials compared to unstimulated trials (12 mice; 2-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov Test, D = 0.078, 95% CI: [0.067,0.093], p = 2.8·10–26).
source: DAN activation significantly early-shifted the distribution of self-timed movements on stimulated trials compared to unstimulated trials (12 mice; 2-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) Test, D = 0.078 (95% CI: [0.067,0.093]), p = 2.8·10–26), whereas inhibition produced significant late-shifting compared to unstimulated trials (4 mice; two-sample KS Test, D = 0.051 (95% CI: [0.034,0.077]), p = 3.1·10–4; Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the optogenetic activation experiments shown in Figure 7B and supplementary figures.

claim: DAN inhibition produced significant late-shifting of self-timed movements compared to unstimulated trials (4 mice; two-sample KS Test, D = 0.051, 95% CI: [0.034,0.077], p = 3.1·10–4).
source: DAN activation significantly early-shifted the distribution of self-timed movements on stimulated trials compared to unstimulated trials (12 mice; 2-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) Test, D = 0.078 (95% CI: [0.067,0.093]), p = 2.8·10–26), whereas inhibition produced significant late-shifting compared to unstimulated trials (4 mice; two-sample KS Test, D = 0.051 (95% CI: [0.034,0.077]), p = 3.1·10–4; Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the optogenetic inhibition experiments shown in Figure 7B and supplementary figures.

claim: Stimulation of mice expressing no opsin produced no consistent effect on timing (5 mice; two-sample KS Test, D = 0.017, 95% CI: [0.015,0.040], p = 0.62).
source: Stimulation of mice expressing no opsin produced no consistent effect on timing (5 mice; two-sample KS Test, D = 0.017 (95% CI: [0.015,0.040]), p = 0.62).
evidence: This is a finding from the no-opsin control experiments.

claim: Optogenetic DAN activation did not elicit immediate licking outside the context of the task.
source: We likewise found that optogenetic DAN activation did not elicit immediate licking outside the context of the task (Figure 7—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from the control experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Optogenetic DAN inhibition did not reduce the rate of spontaneous licking outside the context of the task.
source: Additionally, optogenetic DAN inhibition did not reduce the rate of spontaneous licking outside the context of the task (Figure 7—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from the control experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4B.

claim: The instantaneous GCaMP6f signal alone was a robustly significant predictor of movement state in the probabilistic movement-state decoding model.
source: Initial model selection included previous trial history (movement time and reward outcome history) in addition to the DAN GCaMP6f signal, but Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) analysis indicated that the instantaneous GCaMP6f signal alone was a robustly significant predictor of movement state, whereas previous trial outcomes were insignificant contributors and did not further improve the model (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the model selection analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The continuous DAN GCaMP6f signal was predictive of current movement state at any time t, and it served as a significant predictor of movement state up to at least 2 s in the past.
source: The continuous DAN GCaMP6f signal was indeed predictive of current movement state at any time t, and it served as a significant predictor of movement state up to at least 2 s in the past (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is a finding from the probabilistic movement-state decoding model shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The dopaminergic signal level closer to time t tended to absorb the behavioral variance explained by more distant, previous signal levels.
source: However, the signals became progressively more predictive of the current movement state as time approached t. That is, the dopaminergic signal level closer to time t tended to absorb the behavioral variance explained by more distant, previous signal levels (Figure 8C), reminiscent of how threshold crossing time absorbed the variance explained by the baseline dopaminergic signal in the movement-timing decoding model (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: This is a finding from the probabilistic movement-state decoding model shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The DAN GCaMP6f signals were remarkably predictive of the hazard function, explaining 65% of the variance on average (n = 12 mice).
source: The DAN GCaMP6f signals were remarkably predictive of the hazard function, both for individual sessions and on average, explaining 65% of the variance on average (n = 12 mice).
evidence: This is a finding from the hazard function decoding analysis.

claim: When the model was fit on the same data in which the timepoint identifiers were shuffled, the predictive power was essentially abolished, explaining only 5% of the variance on average.
source: Conversely, when the model was fit on the same data in which the timepoint identifiers were shuffled, this predictive power was essentially abolished, explaining only 5% of the variance on average (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is a finding from the shuffled control analysis shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Dopaminergic ramping could reflect reward expectation.
source: A common feature in these experiments and our self-timed movement task is that trials culminated in the animal's receiving reward. Thus, parsimony suggests that dopaminergic ramping could reflect reward expectation.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the common features across different experimental paradigms.

claim: Dopaminergic ramping is generally absent in Pavlovian paradigms, in which animals learn to expect passive reward delivery at a fixed time following a conditioned stimulus.
source: However, dopaminergic ramping is generally absent in Pavlovian paradigms, in which animals learn to expect passive reward delivery at a fixed time following a conditioned stimulus (Menegas et al., 2015; Tian et al., 2016; Schultz et al., 1997; Starkweather et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on dopaminergic activity in Pavlovian tasks.

claim: Ramping was reported in monkey DANs during a Pavlovian paradigm with reward uncertainty.
source: One exception is a report of ramping activity in monkey DANs during a Pavlovian paradigm with reward uncertainty (Fiorillo et al., 2003); however, ramping was not subsequently reproduced under similar conditions, either in monkeys (Fiorillo, 2011; Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2009; Tobler et al., 2005) or rodents (Hart et al., 2015; Tian and Uchida, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on dopaminergic activity.

claim: The animal actively determines when reward will be delivered/omitted in the self-timed movement task—just after it moves.
source: Although both our task and Pavlovian tasks involve timing, the key difference may be that the animal actively determines when reward will be delivered/omitted in the self-timed movement task—just after it moves.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the key difference between the self-timed movement task and Pavlovian tasks.

claim: Certainty in the timing of reward relative to its own movement would resolve the animal's uncertainty of its position in the value landscape, and may thus explain why dopaminergic ramping occurs prominently in the self-timed movement task, but not in Pavlovian tasks.
source: Certainty in the timing of reward relative to its own movement would resolve the animal's uncertainty of its position in the value landscape, and may thus explain why dopaminergic ramping occurs prominently in the self-timed movement task, but not in Pavlovian tasks (Hamilos and Assad, 2020).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the RPE model framework, with citation to a companion theoretical paper.

claim: Selective optogenetic stimulation or inhibition of DANs generally does not affect reward-related movements on the same trial.
source: In contrast to these equivocal findings, a large body of evidence suggests that selective optogenetic stimulation or inhibition of DANs generally does not affect reward-related movements on the same trial.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from prior literature.

claim: Numerous studies have examined the effects of optogenetic modulation of DANs in Pavlovian conditioning paradigms, with the general finding that DAN modulation affects conditioned movements on subsequent trials or sessions—a learning effect—but not on the same trial.
source: Numerous studies have also examined the effects of optogenetic modulation of DANs in Pavlovian conditioning paradigms, with the general finding that DAN modulation affects conditioned movements on subsequent trials or sessions—a learning effect—but not on the same trial (Coddington and Dudman, 2018; Coddington and Dudman, 2021; Lee et al., 2020; Maes et al., 2020; Morrens et al., 2020; Pan et al., 2021; Saunders et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple prior studies on optogenetic modulation of DANs.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of mouse DANs at the same time as an olfactory conditioned stimulus had no effect on anticipatory licking on the concurrent trial, even though inhibition at the time of reward delivery reduced the probability and rate of anticipatory licking on subsequent trials.
source: For example, Lee et al. found that optogenetic inhibition of mouse DANs at the same time as an olfactory conditioned stimulus had no effect on anticipatory licking on the concurrent trial, even though inhibition at the time of reward delivery reduced the probability and rate of anticipatory licking on subsequent trials (Lee et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: The preponderance of evidence argues against a simple scheme whereby modulating DAN activity leads to a change in motivation that automatically evokes or suppresses reward-related movements in real time.
source: Thus, the preponderance of evidence argues against a simple scheme whereby modulating DAN activity leads to a change in motivation that automatically evokes or suppresses reward-related movements in real time.
evidence: This is an inference based on the review of prior literature and the authors' own findings.

claim: The fact that robust, concurrent optogenetic modulation of movement timing was observed in the self-timed movement task suggests that additional factors were at play for self-timed movements.
source: The fact that we observed robust, concurrent optogenetic modulation of movement timing in our experiment suggests that additional factors were at play for self-timed movements.
evidence: This is an inference based on the contrast between the authors' findings and prior literature.

claim: When DANs were deliberately over-stimulated, 'dyskinetic' body movements were observed rather than purposive licking.
source: However, when we deliberately over-stimulated DANs—eliciting even higher dopamine signals in the DLS (Figure 7—figure supplement 2)—we observed 'dyskinetic' body movements rather than purposive licking.
evidence: This is an observation from the over-stimulation control experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Conditions that increase/decrease dopamine availability or efficacy speed/slow the 'internal clock', respectively.
source: Broadly speaking, conditions that increase/decrease dopamine availability or efficacy speed/slow the 'internal clock', respectively (Dews and Morse, 1958; Mikhael and Gershman, 2019; Schuster and Zimmerman, 1961; Malapani et al., 1998; Meck, 1986; Meck, 2006; Merchant et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior pharmacological and lesion studies on dopamine and timing.

claim: The dopaminergic ramping signals observed bear resemblance to Pacemaker-Accumulator models of neural timing, in which a hypothetical accumulator signals that an interval has elapsed when it reaches a threshold level.
source: The dopaminergic ramping signals we observed also bear resemblance to Pacemaker-Accumulator models of neural timing, in which a hypothetical accumulator signals that an interval has elapsed when it reaches a threshold level (Gallistel and Gibbon, 2000; Lustig and Meck, 2005; Meck, 2006).
evidence: This is a comparison to theoretical models of timing, supported by citations.

claim: To 'self-time' a movement also implies that the movement is prepared and pre-potent during the timing period, potentially making the relevant neural motor circuits more sensitive to dopaminergic modulation.
source: To 'self-time' a movement also implies that the movement is prepared and pre-potent during the timing period, potentially making the relevant neural motor circuits more sensitive to dopaminergic modulation.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism underlying the observed effects.

claim: The authors propose that when a movement is pre-potent (as in the self-timed movement task), dopaminergic signaling can modulate the probability of initiating that movement.
source: Consequently, we propose that when a movement is pre-potent (as in our self-timed movement task), dopaminergic signaling can modulate the probability of initiating that movement.
evidence: This is the authors' proposed interpretation of their findings.

claim: The endogenous ramping dynamics were highly predictive of the moment-by-moment probability of movement (as captured by the hazard function), with DAN signals becoming progressively better predictors as the time of movement onset approached.
source: Consistent with this view, we found that the endogenous ramping dynamics were highly predictive of the moment-by-moment probability of movement (as captured by the hazard function), with DAN signals becoming progressively better predictors as the time of movement onset approached.
evidence: This is a finding from the hazard function analysis.

claim: This view of dopaminergic modulation of movement probability could be related to classic findings from extrapyramidal movement disorders, in which dysfunction of the nigrostriatal pathway produces aberrations in movement initiation rather than paralysis or paresis.
source: This view of dopaminergic modulation of movement probability could be related to classic findings from extrapyramidal movement disorders, in which dysfunction of the nigrostriatal pathway produces aberrations in movement initiation rather than paralysis or paresis (Bloxham et al., 1984; Fahn, 2011; Hallett and Khoshbin, 1980).
evidence: This is an interpretation linking the findings to clinical observations, supported by citations.

claim: When 'spontaneous' licks during the ITI were averaged, noisy, slow ramping signals building over seconds up to the time of the next lick were observed, with a time course related to the duration of the inter-lick interval.
source: However, when we averaged DAN signals aligned to 'spontaneous' licks during the ITI, we also observed noisy, slow ramping signals building over seconds up to the time of the next lick, with a time course related to the duration of the inter-lick interval (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of spontaneous licks shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: DAN signals predict movement timing via two low-dimensional signals: a baseline offset and a ramping dynamic that 'stretches' depending on trial-by-trial movement timing.
source: We found that DAN signals predict movement timing via two low-dimensional signals: a baseline offset and a ramping dynamic that 'stretches' depending on trial-by-trial movement timing.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the encoding model analysis.

claim: Similar stretching of neural responses has been observed before self-timed movement in other brain areas in rats and primates, including the dorsal striatum, lateral interparietal cortex, presupplementary and supplementary motor areas, and dorsomedial frontal cortex.
source: Intriguingly, similar stretching of neural responses has been observed before self-timed movement in other brain areas in rats and primates, including the dorsal striatum (Emmons et al., 2017; Mello et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2018), lateral interparietal cortex (Maimon and Assad, 2006), presupplementary and supplementary motor areas (Mita et al., 2009), and dorsomedial frontal cortex (DMFC; Remington et al., 2018; Sohn et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on neural dynamics in other brain areas.

claim: In DMFC, applying dimensionality reduction to the population responses revealed two lower-dimensional characteristics: the speed at which the population dynamics unfolded was scaled ('stretched') to the length of the produced timing interval, and the population state at the beginning of the self-timed movement interval ('setpoint') was correlated with the timed interval.
source: In the case of DMFC, applying dimensionality reduction to the population responses revealed two lower-dimensional characteristics that resembled our findings in DANs: (1) the speed at which the population dynamics unfolded was scaled ('stretched') to the length of the produced timing interval (Wang et al., 2018), and (2) the population state at the beginning of the self-timed movement interval ('setpoint') was correlated with the timed interval (Remington et al., 2018; Sohn et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on DMFC dynamics.

claim: Recurrent neural network models suggested variation in stretching and setpoint states could be controlled by (unknown) tonic or monotonically-ramping inputs to the cortico-striatal system.
source: Recurrent neural network models suggested variation in stretching and setpoint states could be controlled by (unknown) tonic or monotonically-ramping inputs to the cortico-striatal system (Remington et al., 2018; Sohn et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior modeling studies.

claim: DANs exhibit both baseline (e.g., 'setpoint') signals related to timing, as well as monotonically ramping input during the timing interval.
source: We found that DANs exhibit both baseline (e.g., 'setpoint') signals related to timing, as well as monotonically ramping input during the timing interval.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the study.

claim: Through their role as diffusely-projecting modulators, DANs could potentially orchestrate variations in cortico-striatal dynamics observed during timing behavior.
source: Thus, through their role as diffusely-projecting modulators, DANs could potentially orchestrate variations in cortico-striatal dynamics observed during timing behavior.
evidence: This is a speculation about the broader role of DANs based on the findings.

claim: Ramping DAN signals could also be related to the slow ramping signals that have been observed in the human motor system in anticipation of self-initiated movements, for example, readiness potentials in EEG recordings.
source: Ramping DAN signals could also be related to the slow ramping signals that have been observed in the human motor system in anticipation of self-initiated movements, for example, readiness potentials in EEG recordings (Deecke, 1996; Libet et al., 1983).
evidence: This is a speculation linking the findings to human EEG studies, supported by citations.

claim: In operant tasks in which difficulty is systematically varied over blocks of trials, increased intertrial dopamine in the nucleus accumbens has been associated with higher average reward rate and decreased latency to engage in a new trial, suggesting a link between dopamine and 'motivational vigor'.
source: In operant tasks in which difficulty is systematically varied over blocks of trials, increased intertrial dopamine in the nucleus accumbens has been associated with higher average reward rate and decreased latency to engage in a new trial, suggesting a link between dopamine and 'motivational vigor', the propensity to invest effort in work (Hamid et al., 2016; Mohebi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on dopamine and motivation.

claim: In the self-timed movement task, periods with higher average reward rates had lower average baseline dopaminergic signals and later first-lick times.
source: Intriguingly, we observed the opposite relationship in the self-timed movement task: periods with higher average reward rates had lower average baseline dopaminergic signals and later first-lick times.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: For a given first-lick time (e.g., 3.5–3.75 s), no differences in baseline (or ramping) signals were detected during periods with different average reward rates, such as near the beginning or end of a session.
source: Moreover, for a given first-lick time (e.g., 3.5–3.75 s), we did not detect differences in baseline (or ramping) signals during periods with different average reward rates, such as near the beginning or end of a session.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: The activity of nigrostriatal DANs has been shown to correlate with movement speed, force or frequency during movement bouts and could promote more vigorous movement via push-pull interactions with the direct and indirect pathways.
source: The activity of nigrostriatal DANs has been shown to correlate with these parameters during movement bouts and could promote more vigorous movement via push-pull interactions with the direct and indirect pathways (Barter et al., 2015; da Silva et al., 2018; Mazzoni et al., 2007; Panigrahi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on dopamine and movement vigor.

claim: No consistent differences in force- or speed-related parameters (EMG amplitude, latency between lick initiation and lick-tube contact) were detected as a function of movement time.
source: We looked for movement-related vigor signals, examining both the amplitude of lick-related EMG signals and the latency between lick initiation and lick-tube contact. We detected no consistent differences in these force- or speed-related parameters as a function of movement time; on the contrary, the EMG signals were highly stereotyped irrespective of the first-lick time (data not shown).
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: As DAN activity ramps up, the probability of movement likewise increases.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest that as DAN activity ramps up, the probability of movement likewise increases.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the combined findings.

claim: Different rates of increase in DAN activity lead to shorter or longer elapsed intervals before movement, on average.
source: In this view, different rates of increase in DAN activity lead to shorter or longer elapsed intervals before movement, on average.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Recurrent cortical-basal ganglia–thalamic circuits could act to generate movements 'on their own,' without direct external triggers.
source: One possibility is that recurrent cortical-basal ganglia–thalamic circuits could act to generate movements 'on their own,' without direct external triggers (e.g., a 'go!' cue).
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism.

claim: By providing crucial modulation of cortical-basal ganglia–thalamic circuits, DANs could tune the propensity to make self-timed movements.
source: By providing crucial modulation of these circuits, DANs could tune the propensity to make self-timed movements—and pathological loss of DANs could reduce the production of such movements.
evidence: This is a speculation about the role of DANs.
